newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel press for Hebron deal despite attack.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel press for Hebron deal despite attack.

text.p: Senior Israeli and Palestinian negotiators pressed on into early Thursday to clinch a deal on Hebron, despite an Israeli soldier's shooting spree on Palestinian shoppers in the West Bank town.
Off-duty soldier Noam Friedman sprayed rifle fire into a Hebron market on Wednesday, wounding seven Arabs in what he called an attempt to keep the town from being handed over to Palestinian rule.
Friedman, 22, emptied the clip of his M-16 automatic rifle into the crowded open-air market before other soldiers overpowered him, witnesses said.
"Even after soldiers had wrestled him to the ground he tried to put a second magazine into his gun," said a Reuters cameraman.

Friedman, wearing the skullcap and tassled undershirt of a religious Jew, smirked and shook his fist in police custody after an attack that was condemned by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Israeli leaders.
He said the attack was good for Israel.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai held talks with chief Palestine Liberation Organisation negotiator Mahmoud Abbas at the Tel Aviv home of the American ambassador to prevent the violence from scuttling three months of talks on a deal which would see 80 percent of Hebron handed over to Palestinian self-rule.
Friedman told investigators he wanted to sabotage the handover, Israeli Major-General Uzi Dayan told army radio.
"Hebron is ours now and forever," Freidman told Israel television with a defiance reminiscent of another religious ultranationalist, Yigal Amir, who murdered prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.

"Abraham bought the Cave of the Patriarchs for 400 shekels of silver and nobody will give it back," Friedman told reporters, referring to the biblibal story by which Jews trace their claim to Hebron back 4,000 years.

The Cave, where 29 Moslems were massacred by settler Baruch Goldstein three years ago, is holy to Jews and Moslems. It is slated to remain under Israeli control along with all Jewish holy places after the Israeli redeployment.

The shooting underscored the fragility of the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace process, the volatility of Hebron and the feeling of betrayal of right-wing Jews opposed to returning captured land to Arabs.
The United States deplored the shooting and vowed to continue mediating a settlement on Hebron.
"We in the United States condemn this act in the strongest possible terms," U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross told reporters.

Ross conferred on Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who both condemned the attack, in an effort to arrange a summit between the two to close the Hebron deal quickly.
PLO officials said Mordechai and Abbas were trying to finalise outstanding issues from a 1995 peace accord that would lay the groundwork for a Netanyahu-Arafat summit.

Friedman, from Maale Adumim settlement near Jerusalem, fired for nearly 10 seconds into the vegetable market on Martyrs Street wounding men, women and a youth, witnesses and doctors said. Two of the injured were in critical condition.

Palestinians hurled themselves to the ground shouting "massacre" when the bullets started flying. Soldiers and police, thinking they were under attack, ran to the market from the Avraham Avinu settlement firing, witnesses said. One Palestinian man was apparently hit by them.
The army poured troops into the city and put armoured personnel carriers on surrounding hills to prevent reprisals. It also imposed a curfew which was later lifted.
